scenes.title: Why touching the page is slow
scenes.narration: Every web page is a tree of elements the browser keeps in memory, called the DOM.

steps.say: Changing it by hand is slow. Say our code replaces the list’s inner HTML.
The browser now has to work out every size and position again, then repaint. That is called a reflow.
And each element is not a small thing. One list item carries hundreds of properties, styles and listeners.
Change fifty list items in a loop, read a size after each, and the browser redoes the layout fifty times.
React’s idea: you describe the page for your data, and React makes the fewest changes to get there.

scenes.title: JSX turns into JavaScript
scenes.narration: This looks like HTML, but it is not.

steps.say: Before your code runs, a compiler such as Babel rewrites it into a call.
The tag becomes a call to a function named jsx, with the props and the text as arguments.
So JSX is only a nicer way to write a function call.

scenes.title: What the call returns
scenes.narration: And that call does not draw a button.

steps.say: It returns a plain object that describes one: a React element.
It says the type is a button, and holds the props.
It is just a description, a few bytes in memory. Making thousands is cheap.

scenes.title: Last render and this render
scenes.narration: Each time your data changes, React builds a fresh tree and compares it with the last one.

steps.say: Here is the last tree, and the fresh one beside it.
This time Card 2 has a new text colour.
And there is a new Card 3.

draw.write:
any two trees: n³ steps
1,000 nodes → 1,000,000,000

steps.say: Finding the fewest changes between any two trees takes about n cubed steps. For a thousand elements, a billion.

draw.write: React’s two rules: about n steps

steps.say: So React cheats, with two simple rules, and gets it down to about one step per element.

steps.say: Rule one: if a div became a span, React does not look inside. It throws the old part away.
And it builds the new one, so the counter starts over.
Rule two: in a list, keys say which item is which.
Cat is new at the top, so React adds one item instead of rewriting all three.

scenes.title: Before React 16: one long call stack
scenes.narration: Before React 16, React walked the tree with plain function calls.

steps.say: Rendering App calls render on Dashboard.
Which calls Sidebar.
Which calls NavList. Each call waits for the one below it.
Now the user clicks. But the page’s one thread is busy.
These calls cannot pause. The click waits until every one returns.

scenes.title: A 40 ms render on the main thread

steps.say: The screen wants a new frame sixty times a second, about every sixteen point seven milliseconds.
This update takes forty milliseconds.
And the click lands five milliseconds in.
Two frames go by with nothing new drawn. The page freezes.
Only at forty milliseconds does the click get its turn. Typing feels sticky.

scenes.title: Fiber: a call stack React controls
scenes.narration: React 16 rewrote this as Fiber. Each component gets a small object, a fiber, with three links.

steps.say: Its first child, its next sibling, and its parent, called return.
A loop holds one pointer, work in progress. It starts at App.
It does App’s work, then follows the child link down to Header.
Header has no child, so it follows the sibling link across to Main.
Now a click comes in. The loop just stops. The pointer remembers where it was.
Once the click is handled, it picks up right where it left off, down to Card.
Card has no child and no sibling, so it climbs the return link to Main.
Main has no sibling either, so up again to App. The walk is done.

scenes.narration: Every update now happens in two phases.

steps.say: Render calls your components and works out what changed. Commit applies them.
Render can pause, give up, or start again. Commit never stops once it begins.
Render never touches the page. Commit changes it all in one go.
And straight after, commit updates refs and runs layout effects.

scenes.title: Double buffering: one pointer swap
scenes.narration: React keeps two trees: the one on screen, and the one it is building.

steps.say: The root’s current pointer marks tree A, the one the user sees.
In the background, render builds tree B. The user sees none of it.
When it is done, commit swaps one pointer. Tree B is now current.
So the user never sees a half finished page. Tree A is kept, to build the next update in.

scenes.narration: Let’s follow one update from start to finish.

steps.say: Your code calls set state.
The scheduler decides how urgent it is. A click beats a background fetch.
The reconciler builds the new tree and finds what changed. This is render, and it can pause.
React DOM applies the changes in one go. This is commit.
And the browser paints the new frame.
